question: How would you design a coding task with a deterministic verifier?

scenes.sub: Accept any correct solution. Reject anything that cheats.
scenes.say: Designing a coding task with a verifier. A verifier is a program that checks someone's solution, and says pass or fail. Deterministic means the same answer every run.

scenes.head: Think of a driving test
scenes.say: Think of a driving test. The examiner uses a fixed checklist, the same rules for everyone. The route is a surprise, so you can't memorize it. And any good driver passes, not only someone who drives exactly like the examiner. A coding verifier needs the same three traits.

scenes.head: Example: top k words, ties alphabetical
scenes.say: The task: return the k most frequent words, ties broken alphabetically. The reference counts, then sorts by count and then name. The generator takes a seed, so the same seed always makes the same input. The checker compares the candidate with the reference. The tie rule is in the spec, so exactly one answer is right.

scenes.head: Catching hard-coding
scenes.say: Now the cheater. This solution hard-codes the sample. It passes the visible example. But hidden seeded tests it has never seen fail. Large inputs with a time limit catch slow brute force. Edge cases, like empty input, go in on purpose.

scenes.head: When many answers are correct

panels.code:
def check_pair(nums, target, out):
    i, j = out
    return (i != j
            and 0 <= i < len(nums)
            and 0 <= j < len(nums)
            and nums[i] + nums[j] == target)

scenes.say: Some problems allow several correct answers, like two sum with many valid pairs. Then don't compare with the reference output. The checker validates: two different indices, both in range, and the values add up to the target. That accepts any correct solution.

scenes.head: In the interview: follow-ups
rows: How do you know the reference is right?
Cross-check against a slow brute force on small random inputs.
Reproducible failures; same tests every run.
Write a checker that validates, don't compare text.
Vague spec, or only testing the sample.
scenes.say: Likely follow-ups. How do you know the reference is right? Cross-check against a slow brute force on small random inputs. Why seeds? Reproducible failures. Many valid answers? Validate, don't compare text. The common mistake: a vague spec, or only testing the sample.

lines: A precise spec, a trusted reference, and seeded tests.
When many answers are correct, I validate instead of comparing text.
Hidden tests, edge cases and time limits stop hard-coding.
